current_episode.title: Putting literacy and assessment at the heart of student transition

guest.titre: Director of English, School Improvement Team
guest.bio_context: Talia Caralambos relocated to the North East in April after training and teaching English and Media at Ritchie Diver Secondary School in London. She comes from a bilingual household and taught English in India at age 17, which she says sparked her lifelong commitment to equity and education through literacy. As Director of English at Laidlaw Schools Trust, she supports curriculum development and literacy improvement across 11 schools serving communities with high mobility, economic disadvantage, and over 60 languages spoken in some settings.

context.real_quote: Don't wait until a child is failing to act. You need to diagnose on entry, involve staff from the start, and if you're fortunate enough to have digital tools that you can access, align that to your transition work, because it can be transformational.

pending_qa.q: How does the Bishop Wilkinson Catholic Education Trust structure its primary-to-secondary transition programme?
pending_qa.r: Bishop Wilkinson Catholic Education Trust begins transition at the end of Year 5 with a large event called the Bishop Wilkinson Celebration of Sport at Gateshead Stadium, bringing together Year 5 children from all 42 primary schools. Throughout Year 6, contextual data including attendance, special needs information, and reading results are shared between primaries and secondaries. Year 6 pupils sit the NGRT in their primary school over a three-week window in May and June after their SATs, so that by mid-June all initial diagnostic data is available before September.

pending_qa.q: Why does Bishop Wilkinson Catholic Education Trust administer NGRT in Year 6 rather than waiting until September of Year 7?
pending_qa.r: Graeme Finlay explains that previously some secondary schools were administering the NGRT in September, which created a lag between identifying children who needed further diagnostics and getting support in place. By moving the test to May and June in primary school, the trust can identify children needing support over the summer, allow secondary reading leaders to plan provision in advance, and ensure intervention is in place from the very first week of secondary school — avoiding the stigma of late-stage identification.

pending_qa.q: What is the 'six-week dip' in the context of student transition, and how do these trusts address it?
pending_qa.r: The 'six-week dip' refers to the period after summer where students readjust to school routines and may lose academic momentum, particularly in reading. Talia Caralambos highlights this is especially acute for bilingual and EAL learners who may go the entire summer without communicating in English with an adult. Laidlaw Schools Trust addresses this by assessing students on NGRT before summer and front-loading literacy support from September, rather than waiting to see if a dip occurs.

pending_qa.q: What advice do transition programme leaders give to educators building their own primary-to-secondary literacy transition plan?
pending_qa.r: Graeme Finlay advises careful liaison with GL Assessment over several months to design a reading strategy before identifying tools, and stresses the importance of being supported to interpret diagnostic data so that the right questions are asked of the right people at the right time. Talia Caralambos advises educators to 'diagnose on entry, involve staff from the start,' align digital tools to transition work, and never put a ceiling on pupils — framing literacy as a human right.

pending_qa.q: How can CAT4 and NGRT be used together to support student transition and identify underachievement?
pending_qa.r: Georgina Cook and Emma Dibden explain that combining CAT4 verbal reasoning scores with NGRT reading results allows educators to compare a student's reading attainment against their cognitive potential. Where scores do not align — captured through statistically generated discrepancy categories — it signals a need for closer investigation. The discrepancy categories are based on distributions from large datasets: the expected range covers the middle 50% of score differences, the next 15% on either side are deemed higher or lower than expected, and the top or bottom 10% are classified as much higher or much lower than expected.

pending_qa.q: What is the Standard Age Score (SAS) and why is it recommended for comparing reading assessment results across students?
pending_qa.r: The Standard Age Score (SAS) is the score recommended by GL Assessment when making comparisons across any norm-referenced test, as it allows educators to see how students are performing relative to the national average in a fair, age-adjusted way. Georgina Cook highlights that using the SAS is the fairest approach when comparing results from tests such as CAT4 and NGRT across different cohorts or contexts.

pending_qa.q: What percentage of Bishop Wilkinson Catholic Education Trust's secondary school pupils come from its own primary schools?
pending_qa.r: Around 70% of pupils in Bishop Wilkinson Catholic Education Trust's secondary schools come from the trust's own primary schools. Graeme Finlay describes this as a 'really unique opportunity to form the education of children right through their entire schooling,' from age 3 through to age 18 at sixth form, across 47 schools in four local authorities.
